claim: Natural populations can contain multiple types of coexisting individuals.
source: Natural populations can contain multiple types of coexisting individuals.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural populations presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cyclic dominance is a popular theoretical basis for the maintenance of diversity.
source: A popular theoretical basis for the maintenance of diversity is cyclic dominance, illustrated by the rock-paper-scissor game.
evidence: This statement reflects established theoretical understanding in the field.

claim: It appears difficult to find cyclic dominance in nature.
source: However, it appears difficult to find cyclic dominance in nature.
evidence: This is an observation about the empirical difficulty of finding cyclic dominance, supported by the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: The chance for cyclic dominance to emerge is lower when the newly introduced type is similar to existing types compared to the introduction of an unrelated type.
source: Our results showed that the chance for cyclic dominance to emerge is lower when the newly introduced type is similar to existing types compared to the introduction of an unrelated type.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' theoretical model and simulations.

claim: Cyclic dominance is more likely to evolve through the assembly of unrelated types whereas it rarely evolves within a community of similar types.
source: This suggests that cyclic dominance is more likely to evolve through the assembly of unrelated types whereas it rarely evolves within a community of similar types.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results presented in the study.

claim: Some individuals compete with each other to exploit a shared resource.
source: Some individuals compete with each other to exploit a shared resource (Hardin, 1960; Connell, 1983), whereas others coexist (Morris et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Interactions affect the death or reproduction of individuals and thus shape the composition of populations.
source: Interactions affect the death or reproduction of individuals and thus shape the composition of populations (Friedman and Gore, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Different types of individuals are distinguishable at the interaction level and they have a complex interaction structure.
source: Different types of individuals are distinguishable at the interaction level and they have a complex interaction structure (Farahpour et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Interaction structures themselves can support the coexistence of multiple types.
source: Because interaction structures themselves can support the coexistence of multiple types, they have been extensively studied in ecology and evolution (Gross et al., 2009; Allesina and Levine, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In cyclic dominance, each type dominates another one but is in turn dominated by a separate type, leading to a Rock-Paper-Scissors cycle.
source: A particularly exciting type of interaction is cyclic dominance, in which each type dominates another one but is in turn dominated by a separate type, leading to a Rock-Paper-Scissors cycle (Maynard Smith, 1982; Hofbauer et al., 1998; Szab and Fth, 2007) as sketched in Figure 1A.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In cyclic dominance, none of the types fixates in the population because each type is dominated by one type while it simultaneously dominates a third type.
source: None of the types fixates in the population, because each type is dominated by one type while it simultaneously dominates a third type.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the definition of cyclic dominance.

claim: Cyclic dominance can support biodiversity.
source: Thus, it has been argued that this type of interaction can support biodiversity (Reichenbach et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cyclic dominance has attracted substantial attention and has been extensively studied theoretically.
source: Cyclic dominance has therefore attracted substantial attention and it has been extensively studied theoretically (Maynard Smith, 1982; Hofbauer et al., 1998; Frean and Abraham, 2001; Hauert et al., 2002; Reichenbach et al., 2007; Szab and Fth, 2007; Mathiesen et al., 2011; Jiang et al., 2011; Allesina and Levine, 2011; Szolnoki et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Toxin production in Escherichia coli is a famous example of cyclic dominance in biology.
source: A famous example of this type of cyclic dominance in biology is toxin production in Escherichia coli (Kerr et al., 2002; Kirkup and Riley, 2004; Cascales et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Toxin-producing E. coli cells can purge cells that are sensitive to the toxin.
source: Toxin-producing (or colicinogenic) E. coli cells can purge cells that are sensitive to the toxin.
evidence: This is a description of the biological interaction in E. coli, supported by the context and citations.

claim: Toxin-producing E. coli are dominated by resistant cells that do not produce the toxin.
source: However such toxin producers are dominated by resistant cells that do not produce the toxin.
evidence: This is a description of the biological interaction in E. coli, supported by the context and citations.

claim: Resistant E. coli cells are dominated by sensitive cells, which avoid the costs of resistance.
source: Once common, resistant cells are again dominated by sensitive cells, which avoid the costs of resistance.
evidence: This is a description of the biological interaction in E. coli, supported by the context and citations.

claim: The mating strategies of North American side-blotched lizards Uta stansburiana exhibit cyclic dominance.
source: Another example is the mating strategies of North American side-blotched lizards Uta stansburiana (Sinervo and Lively, 1996).

claim: In side-blotched lizards, the strategy of males guarding several females dominates the strategy of males guarding only a single female.
source: The strategy of males guarding several females dominates the strategy of males guarding only a single female.
evidence: This is a description of the mating strategy dynamics in lizards, supported by the context and citations.

claim: In side-blotched lizards, sneaky strategies can become dominant over the strategy of males guarding several females.

evidence: This is a description of the mating strategy dynamics in lizards, supported by the context and citations.

claim: In side-blotched lizards, once the sneaky strategy is common, the strategy of guarding only a single female can be successful again.
source: Once such a sneaky strategy is common, the strategy of guarding only a single female can be successful again leading to cyclic dominance among the mating types as illustrated in Figure 1C.
evidence: This is a description of the mating strategy dynamics in lizards, supported by the context, citations, and Figure 1C.

source: In addition to E. coli and side-blotched lizards, other examples of cyclic dominance have been described in ecology: Stylopoma spongites (Jackson and Buss, 1975), Drosophila melanogaster (Clark et al., 2000), European lizards Lacerta vivipara (Sinervo et al., 2007), and plant systems (Taylor, 1990; Lankau and Strauss, 2007; Cameron et al., 2009).

claim: Examples of cyclic dominance have been described in Drosophila melanogaster.

claim: Examples of cyclic dominance have been described in European lizards Lacerta vivipara.

claim: Rareness of cyclic dominance is found in both soil bacteria and plant systems.
